title: MYP Language and Literature Revision for eAssessment
summary: MYP Language and Literature revision made practical. Learn what to practise, how to self-assess with the criteria, and how to manage exam time.
body_markdown:
MYP Language and Literature revision becomes much easier once you stop treating English as a subject you can only improve by “writing more.” Effective preparation is more deliberate. You need to analyse unfamiliar texts, produce literary and non-literary writing, assess your work against the criteria, and complete all of this under time pressure.


The Language and Literature eAssessment is a two-hour on-screen examination. It tests how well you can interpret choices made by other writers and creators, then make purposeful choices in your own writing. The best preparation therefore alternates between reading, writing, feedback, and timed practice.


RevisionDojo’s[MYP English Language and Literature resources](https://www.revisiondojo.com/myp/myp-english-langlit) bring these activities together through Study Notes, Flashcards, practice questions, and AI-supported feedback.


### Your MYP Language and Literature revision checklist


A balanced preparation plan should include:


- analysing unfamiliar literary, non-literary, and visual texts
- explaining effects rather than merely identifying techniques
- practising literary writing from visual prompts
- producing non-literary text types for specific audiences and purposes
- learning how Criteria A-D describe successful work
- completing timed responses on a computer
- reviewing feedback and rewriting weak sections


The important word is *balanced* . A student who knows twenty literary techniques but cannot explain their effects is not fully prepared. Neither is a fluent creative writer who has never practised an analytical response against the clock.


### Understand what the eAssessment asks you to do


The examination lasts 120 minutes and contains three broad areas of work: unseen-text analysis, literary production, and non-literary production. RevisionDojo’s guide to the[MYP English Language and Literature eAssessment structure](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/myp-english-language-literature-eassessment-structure) explains the task arrangement and mark allocation in greater detail.


The format reveals something useful about revision. You are not preparing to reproduce memorised essays. You are preparing to make good decisions when the source, image, audience, or purpose is unfamiliar.


Begin by reviewing the[topics covered in MYP English Language and Literature](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/what-topics-are-covered-myp-english-language-literature) . Then divide each study session between one receptive skill, such as analysis, and one productive skill, such as writing an opening or planning an article.


### Practise analysis as a chain of reasoning


Weak analysis often resembles a collection of labels: metaphor, short sentence, dark colour, rhetorical question. The labels may be correct, but naming a choice is only the beginning.


Use this reasoning chain instead:


**Choice → evidence → effect → meaning → purpose**


For example, do not stop after noticing that an advertisement uses direct address. Explain how the pronoun places responsibility on the viewer, how that shapes the tone, and why it supports the creator’s purpose.


During MYP Language and Literature practice, rotate among prose extracts, poetry, speeches, advertisements, articles, and multimodal texts. Ask the same questions each time:


- What is the creator trying to make the audience think, feel, or do?
- Which language, structural, and visual choices support that purpose?
- How do the choices work together?
- What precise evidence supports my interpretation?


The[media construction study resources](https://www.revisiondojo.com/myp/myp-english-langlit/myp-english-langlit-media-construction) can help you practise examining the relationship between visual design, language, audience, and purpose.


### Build adaptable writing skills


Creative preparation should not mean memorising a complete story and forcing it onto any prompt. Build a small toolkit instead: methods for establishing voice, shifting pace, describing setting, creating tension, and ending with significance.


For a visual stimulus, spend a few minutes deciding what the image suggests beyond its literal content. A doorway might suggest opportunity, exclusion, or uncertainty. Your interpretation gives the writing direction. The[describing place notes and activities](https://www.revisiondojo.com/myp/myp-english-langlit/myp-english-langlit-describing-place) are useful when setting needs to carry mood or meaning.


Non-literary writing requires a different kind of flexibility. Practise articles, speeches, letters, reviews, and opinion pieces, but focus on the decisions underneath the format:


- Who is the audience?
- What is the purpose?
- What register is appropriate?
- Which structural conventions will help?
- What response should the ending produce?


A speech and an article may discuss the same issue, yet their openings, transitions, direct address, and conclusions should feel different. Text type is not decoration. It is part of how meaning reaches an audience.


A student gives a crowned timer authority over an overlong introduction


### Use Criteria A-D to self-assess


The four criteria are **A: Analysing** , **B: Organizing** , **C: Producing text** , and **D: Using language** . Read RevisionDojo’s full explanation of the[MYP Language and Literature assessment criteria](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/criteria-for-myp-english-language-and-literature) alongside the descriptors supplied by your school.


### Criterion A: Analysing


Check whether you have interpreted the text, supported ideas with evidence, explained the effects of choices, and compared features when required. Highlight every sentence that genuinely explains *how* or *why* . If a paragraph contains mostly plot summary or labels, revise it.


### Criterion B: Organizing


Look at the response from a distance. Does the sequence make sense? Does each paragraph advance the central idea? Is the structure appropriate for the text type? Planning should make your argument or purpose visible before you begin drafting.


### Criterion C: Producing text


Ask whether your ideas show imagination, insight, and deliberate stylistic choices. A successful response does not simply include techniques. Its choices work together to create a coherent effect for an intended audience.


### Criterion D: Using language


Review vocabulary, sentence variety, grammar, punctuation, spelling, and register. Correctness matters, but suitability matters too. Elaborate vocabulary is not automatically effective if a simpler word would be more precise.


After every practice response, select one descriptor from each relevant criterion and record one piece of evidence that you met it. Then choose one specific improvement. “Use better language” is vague; “replace repeated verbs and correct three comma splices” gives you something actionable.


### Manage the 120 minutes deliberately


Time management improves through rehearsal, not hope. A sensible starting model is:


- 40-45 minutes for unseen-text analysis
- 25-30 minutes for literary writing
- 35-40 minutes for non-literary writing
- 5-10 minutes for final checks


This is a practice model, not a compulsory IB rule. Adjust it using your school’s guidance, the demands of the examination, and evidence from your own timed work. RevisionDojo’s guide to the[MYP English Language and Literature eAssessment length](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/myp-english-language-literature-eassessment-length) provides further context for planning the two hours.


Use checkpoints during mock sessions. If an analysis paragraph is consuming too much time, complete its central reasoning and move forward. An unfinished examination is rarely improved by a perfect introduction.


Practise on screen because typing changes pacing. Complete short timed drills first, then full mock examinations. RevisionDojo’s Questionbank and grading tools can support repeated attempts, while Study Notes, Flashcards, and AI Chat help diagnose gaps between attempts. You can also explore the wider[MYP subject resource directory](https://www.revisiondojo.com/myp) when planning revision across your complete timetable.


### A practical two-week preparation plan


During the first week, concentrate on accuracy. Complete three short analyses, one literary response, and two non-literary plans. Self-assess each attempt with the relevant criteria, then rewrite the weakest paragraph or section.


During the second week, introduce pressure. Complete two extended timed practices on screen, leaving several days between them. Use the interval to study recurring weaknesses rather than immediately attempting another full examination.


The goal is not to feel endlessly busy. It is to create a feedback loop: attempt, assess, improve, and repeat. That loop is where confidence comes from.


MYP Language and Literature rewards purposeful choices. RevisionDojo makes those choices easier to practise by connecting clear notes, active-recall Flashcards, targeted questions, AI Chat, grading support, and mock-style preparation in one place. When exam day arrives, the task should not feel predictable, but your method should.
